description:
Creativity, technology, and a thirst for knowledge.

We are a driven team that isn't afraid of complex challenges and picks up new skills fast. We thrive in the tech space and build projects with a fresh perspective!
summary:
OUTPOST is a co-op Roblox game for ages 7–12 in which a crew of up to four keeps a Mars base, Research Station Alpha, alive for 30 Martian days (Sols). Players wear spacesuits with limited air, share exactly 120 meals and 120 water rations, repair life-support machines with scarce Materials, and shelter from dust storms and solar storms. Four hands-on research missions (Storm Chasers, Space Garden, Radiation Hunters, Rock Detectives) teach the scientific method through real NASA science.
It addresses the challenge by turning real mission constraints into gameplay. Sprinting costs air and food, going outside risks injury, and low power causes blackouts that drain oxygen. No choice is free. This matters because kids rarely see the decision-making behind space missions, only the outcomes. OUTPOST lets them experience how mission planners trade power, oxygen, radiation protection and time. Every real fact is labelled as NASA science, and everything simulated is marked as part of the game.
details:
What it does. Players survive 30 Sols and finish four research missions. A shared top HUD shows Energy, Oxygen, Water, Food, Materials and crew health. Machines wear out, and players repair them with the right tool and Materials. Dust storms reduce solar power. Low Energy makes lights flicker, and zero Energy causes a blackout in which oxygen slowly falls. Solar storms force the crew to shelter in the safest room. The game ends in Victory, Defeat or Mission Incomplete, with a final report on Sols survived, research accuracy, key decisions, crew condition and base condition.

Research missions:

  • Storm Chasers: plant weather poles, record a dust storm, clean a solar test panel. Players learn that dust cuts solar power.
  • Space Garden: grow two plants and change only ONE thing. Players learn fair experiments and growing food on Mars.
  • Radiation Hunters: place radiation badges and map rooms during a solar storm. Players learn which places protect people best.
  • Rock Detectives: drill samples, use the microscope, photograph wind erosion, and compare with real Curiosity rover photos.

Results are scored on scientific accuracy: how well the evidence supports the player’s conclusion.

Benefits and intended impact. Kids learn real Mars facts (thin atmosphere, about −60 °C, strong radiation, gravity 38 % of Earth’s). They also learn the scientific method (hypothesis, fair test, evidence, conclusion), resource planning, teamwork, and cause and effect: fix the cause, not just the symptom.

Creativity. The trade-off is the core mechanic, not a quiz layer. Science and survival depend on each other: mission rewards (Materials, a cleaner Solar Array, a better Greenhouse, shielding) keep the base alive. Defeat is not punishing. The final report shows the crew’s decisions so players can try a different plan.

Accessibility and design. Minimal interface: one top HUD bar, one instruction line, a six-slot inventory and large buttons. It plays on Roblox on PC, tablet, phone and gamepad.

Tools and technology. Roblox Studio and Luau. The server decides every result and the client only displays it. Survival, supplies, sounds, tutorials and the intro are data-driven, so balancing is easy. Streaming keeps performance smooth.

Factors we considered. We kept to a few core resources so young players aren’t overwhelmed. We avoided any “safe” choice with no cost. We chose accuracy over visual polish in the mechanics. We labelled real and simulated content clearly, and we don’t present static data as live.

Next steps. Connect live NASA DONKI space weather to in-game solar storms, add OSDR astronaut health findings as discovery cards, add Earth–Mars message delay as a new trade-off, and build a classroom mode.
